analysis.investment_thesis: Bajaj Electricals is a stagnant consumer brand with 0.6% revenue CAGR over 9 years, negative operating margins, and D/E of 0.85 — trading at an absurd 120x P/E that cannot be justified by any reasonable earnings path. A business that earns ₹133 Cr on ₹4,826 Cr revenue and is priced at ₹4,525 Cr market cap is not a compounder — it is a value trap in disguise.
key_strengths: Bajaj brand equity with multi-decade consumer trust across fans, appliances, and lighting — a household name
Promoter holding stable at 62.7% with no evidence of stake reduction
Debt dramatically reduced from ₹1,084 Cr (2020) to ₹215 Cr (2025); OCF positive all 5 years
key_risks: Valuation is absurd — 120x trailing P/E on a business with 2.3% net profit CAGR over 9 years
Operating margin is negative at -2.10%; ROE of 7.12% is far below my 15% minimum threshold
Zero revenue growth — ₹4,590 Cr in 2016 vs ₹4,826 Cr in 2025 (0.6% CAGR) with violent year-to-year swings
red_flags: D/E of 0.85 — more than 2.8x my hard limit of 0.3; completely unacceptable
Negative operating margin (-2.10%) means the core business is not generating operating profit
Free cash flow halved from ₹871 Cr (2022) to ₹318 Cr (2025) — deteriorating conversion
Net profit of ₹133 Cr on ₹4,826 Cr revenue = 2.7% net margin; this is not a quality consumer business
Equity dropped from ₹1,907 Cr (2023) to ₹1,441 Cr (2024) — unexplained erosion of ₹466 Cr in one year
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Bajaj Electricals fails almost every test I apply before putting money to work. Revenue has gone nowhere in nine years — ₹4,590 Cr in 2016 to ₹4,826 Cr in 2025, a 0.6% CAGR that does not even keep up with inflation. The business swings between profit and loss (a ₹10 Cr loss in FY20, ₹189 Cr profit in FY21, back to ₹133 Cr in FY25) — this volatility tells me the business model has no durable pricing power or structural advantage. A negative operating margin of -2.10% means the company is destroying value at the operating level, sustained only by other income of ₹76 Cr. When other income props up reported profit, I get very cautious.

The valuation is perhaps the biggest offense. At ₹4,525 Cr market cap and ₹133 Cr net profit, the market is pricing this at 34x book and 120x earnings for a business with no growth. The forward P/E of 28.75x implies a heroic earnings recovery that the last decade gives me no reason to believe in. Add a D/E of 0.85 — nearly three times my hard limit — and an ROE of just 7.12% (I want 18%+), and this stock checks none of my boxes. The Bajaj brand is real, and the debt cleanup from ₹1,084 Cr to ₹215 Cr is commendable, but good brands are not enough when the economics are broken and the price is unjustifiable.
